title: Three quarters of the confirmed maternity billing changes have already happened (and 90% of payers haven't even announced yet)
summary: Our maternity billing resource tracks over 3000 health plans. 181 have confirmed how they are moving off global maternity billing. Of the 127 that committed to a date, 96 have already taken effect. Only 31 land on January 1, 2027. The transition most teams are planning for is mostly behind them.
body_markdown:
Most planning for the end of global OB billing is pointed at January 1, 2027.


We track over 3000 health plans. **181 have confirmed how they are moving off global maternity billing.** Of the 181, 127 actually committed to a transition date.


**96 of those 127 dates have already passed.** Only 31 land on January 1, 2027.


Three quarters of the confirmed transition is behind us, not ahead.


## The dates that already passed


Effective dateConfirmed transitionsMarch 1, 20263May 15, 20262May 31, 20264June 1, 202617 **September 1, 202670** January 1, 202731 (still ahead)


September 1 was the single biggest day of this entire transition, by a wide margin, and it was seven weeks ago.


There is also a category that does not appear on that table at all: **54 plans have confirmed they are transitioning but have not said when.** They are committed, dateless, and could name a date at any point.


## Which raises an uncomfortable question


If a payer in your contract mix moved on September 1, what has been going out on your maternity claims since then?


Not a hypothetical for most organizations. Seventy confirmed transitions took effect that day.


## Why this goes unnoticed


None of this is anyone's fault, and it is not a sign of a team asleep at the wheel. The structure makes it almost invisible.


**The notice does not arrive as an alarm.** Payer policy updates land in provider bulletins, portal announcements and manual revisions. Dozens arrive a month. The one that restructures maternity billing looks exactly like the one that changes a prior auth fax number.


**Nothing breaks loudly.** A claim billed the old way after a payer has moved does not necessarily reject at the clearinghouse. It gets accepted, adjudicated, and paid at a different amount, or denied weeks later in a queue that someone works by payer rather than by service line.


**Nobody owns payer policy monitoring.** The CFO owns the revenue, revenue cycle owns the claims, coding owns the rules, the OB service line owns the patients, and payer contracting owns the relationships. Watching bulletins for maternity-specific changes is not in any of those job descriptions.


**Obstetrics has a long tail.** Because global OB spans most of a pregnancy, a change that took effect in June is still producing claims in February. The exposure does not end when the date passes.


## What to actually do about it


This is the most recoverable money in the entire transition, because it has already happened and the claims still exist. Four steps, in order.


### 1. Build the date list first


For every payer you contract with, write down one thing: the date their maternity billing change took effect, or that they have not said. You cannot audit anything without this, and most organizations do not have it in one place.


### 2. Pull the maternity claims filed after each date


Start with September 1, 2026. That is where 70 of the confirmed transitions sit, so that is where the volume is. Then work backwards through June 1 and the spring dates.


### 3. Separate the three failure modes


They need different fixes.


**Paid at a different rate.** The claim went through, and the payment is not what the contract implies. This is the quietest and usually the largest.


**Denied and reworked.** Someone already fixed these by hand. Worth counting, because the rework cost is the argument for automating the next wave.


**Denied and never reworked.** Small dollar maternity denials that fell below whatever threshold your team works. These are the ones nobody has looked at.


### 4. Fix the edits before January, not after


31 confirmed transitions land on January 1, and 54 more are committed without a date. Put each one into the claim edits ahead of time. The alternative is discovering the change through denials, which is how the last three waves were discovered.


## The timing problem that makes this genuinely hard


A pregnancy runs roughly nine months. These billing changes take effect partway through.


So for any patient pregnant across an effective date, three dates matter: when care began, when her payer switched, and when the claim goes out. They are frequently on different sides of the change, and the correct way to bill depends on which rule the payer applies to which of those dates.


Payers differ on exactly that question. Some key the change to the date of service, some to the first prenatal visit, some to the delivery or due date, and some to where the pregnancy is in its course. A dozen payers, each with its own date and its own rule, is not something a billing team can carry in their heads. It has to live in the edits.


## Where this comes from


We track 4,005 health plans and research their maternity billing policies continuously. 299 have a published policy record so far: 181 confirmed, 57 proposed, 61 describing current policy only. Proposed and current are never counted as a confirmed 2027 transition.


Every organization we could find that delivers babies has a public page listing its payers, what each has published, the effective date, and a link to the source. Free, no form, no sign-up. Someone works this list every day.


[The 2027 Maternity Resource Center](https://www.substrateai.com/payers/2027-substrate-maternity-resource-center)
